interactions.summary: Jiang tests mathematical beauty against the Mona Lisa by asking not only what transcends but what preserves human feeling, concluding that exclusively inhabiting abstract design for too long would be spiritually risky.

claims.claim: A student testimony Jiang allows into the record is that mathematical beauty and symmetry moved someone from atheism toward religion, showing that number and design can indeed carry spiritual pressure.
Jiang's test for superior beauty is not endless complexity alone but whether prolonged attention preserves recognizable human feeling rather than dissolving it.
Jiang implies that an experience which evacuates individuality too completely can become problematic even if it feels transcendental, whereas human art offers company and emotional reciprocity.

signature_moments.moment: The student articulates the attraction of pure mathematical transcendence as the moment when individuality leaves and one tries to be with the mind of God.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It marks the exact temptation Jiang wants to qualify rather than simply deny.

signature_moments.moment: The Mona Lisa wins because she offers company, not just infinity.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This compact phrase captures Jiang's preference for beauty that remains relationally human.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture qualifies its earlier mathematics-to-God line by insisting that fully human art remains safer and richer than long habitation in abstract infinity alone.

uncertainty_notes.note: The conversion narrative is secondhand and anecdotal; the durable content here is Jiang's evaluative distinction between abstract transcendence and humanly embodied beauty.
